editorial:
If you want a movie that will make you angry and hopeful at the same time, this one delivers. It follows Bryan Stevenson, a Harvard-trained lawyer who moves to Alabama to help people on death row who cannot afford good legal help. His biggest case is Walter McMillian, a man sentenced to death for a murder he did not commit, even though the evidence clearly shows he was somewhere else. The story shows how the justice system can fail people, especially when race and poverty are involved, and how one person's determination can slowly push back against that.

The acting is strong across the board, with Michael B. Jordan and Jamie Foxx carrying the emotional weight without overdoing it. The pacing is steady and serious, so it never feels like a fast thriller, but it keeps you invested the whole way through. Some scenes are hard to watch because of the unfairness on screen, and the movie can feel heavy at times. Still, it is a powerful watch for anyone who cares about true stories and justice.
endingExplained: In the final scenes, Bryan presents the evidence that proves Walter was not at the crime scene, and the court finally overturns Walter's conviction. Walter walks free after years on death row, and the movie closes with Bryan continuing his work through the Equal Justice Initiative. The twist is that the real killer was never properly pursued, showing how the system rushed to blame an innocent man. Walter's freedom is a victory, but it also highlights how many others may still be wrongly imprisoned.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves true stories about justice and powerful dramas.
